Sole possession of first place in the NFC North is on the line at Ford Field as two 8-2 rivals clash on Thanksgiving with long winning streaks

        In the first of three Thanksgiving day games, the Detroit Lions play host to the division rival Chicago Bears in one of the biggest games of the NFL season to date.Detroit enters this game winners of six straight and sitting in first place in the NFC North with an 8-2 record. The Lions sport one of the NFL's most efficient and explosive offenses, and their efense hasn't allowed more than 21 points in a game since all the way back in Week 4. The Lions are dealing with injury issues on that side of the ball, but they've held up surprisingly well. That will be put to the test on Thursday afternoon.Chicago comes into this game having won five in a row and sporting an 8-2 record that matches that of Detroit, with the Bears sitting in second place in the division by virtue of a tiebreaker. The Bears also have one of the league's best offenses, while the defense has been strengthened by the acquisition of superstar defensive lineman Jeffery Simmons, who seems to have transformed the unit up front and allowed everything else to click properly into place. That unit, too, will be tested more than ever here.Which of these two teams will keep its winning streak alive and lay claim to sole possession of first place in the division? We'll find out soon enough. Before we break down the matchup, here's a look at how you can watch the game.
Where to watch Lions vs. Bears liveDate: Thursday, Nov. 26 | Time: 1 p.m. ETLocation: Ford Field (Detroit)TV: CBS | Streaming: Paramount+Follow: CBS Sports AppOdds: Bears -2.5, O/U 55.5 via DraftKings Sportsbook When the Bears have the ballChicago is eighth in total yards and eighth in total points this season, but some of that has to do with volume. The Bears rank a surprising 14th in yards per play, 12th in points per drive and 15th in EPA per play, according to Tru Media. Some of that is due to the fact that Caleb Williams missed several games with a hamstring injury, but even with Williams on the field the Bears' EPA per play mark is only the equivalent of the 10th-best offense in the league. Chicago is one of the league's most run-oriented offenses, ranking ninth in the share of plays that turn into a rush attempt. But D'Andre Swift is averaging just 3.7 yards per carry and Kyle Monangai, who has been more effective (5.0 per carry) has played in only five games.The Lions have sported a top run defense this season in allowing only 4.0 yards per carry, but that defense took a couple of massive hits over the last few weeks with the losses of Jack Campbell and Aidan Hutchinson to injury. Still, Detroit held Tampa Bay's running backs to 84 yards on 22 carries last Sunday, when Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell had previously been destroying teams on the ground. The Bears will need Swift and Monangai to find more success if they want to control the game in the fashion they have preferred since Ben Johnson became head coach last year.
Chicago's passing game has been relatively inconsistent this year, as there have been times when Caleb Williams has looked like an elite quarterback and others when he has looked ordinary — sometimes within the same game. (Like the Sunday night showdown against the Buccaneers, for example.) Williams has completed 68.3% of his passes at 7.9 yards per attempt, but he's thrown only 10 touchdown passes against six interceptions. He's 11th in the NFL in EPA per dropback, according to Tru Media, but he's been highly susceptible against the blitz: he ranks fourth in EPA against four-man rushes but only checks in 19th when opponents rush five or more. Detroit has blitzed at a below-average rate this season (30.3%, per Tru Media), but would be wise to turn up the pressure a bit against a quarterback who has shown that he can be pressured into some bad decisions on occasion if you get defenders into his lap.Still, the Lions have been highly susceptible to opposing passing attacks, even if they have been improved since the return of Brian Branch and should get another lift as Kerby Joseph rounds into form. The Lions are 27th in EPA per dropback allowed, and they're in the bottom third in opponents' explosive play rate through the air.
Detroit is most vulnerable against opposing tight ends, allowing the league's fifth-highest target share to the position, so this could be a game where the Bears finally get Colston Loveland going in a way that they haven't been able to accomplish as much as they likely wanted to this year. The Lions do limit yards after the catch better than any defense in the NFL, though, allowing only 4.0 YAC per completion, according to Tru Media. That could take away from some of Chicago's success in the screen game and possibly limit the effectiveness of Luther Burden III and — to a lesser extent because he's not as big a part of the offense — Kalif Raymond.When the Lions have the ballThe Lions are third in the NFL in yards and fifth in points. They're fifth in both yards per play and points per drive, as well as fifth in EPA per play, according to Tru Media. They're second in EPA per pass attempt and third in EPA per rush attempt. They're third in passing success rate, first in rushing success rate and third in overall success rate. They are, in other words, a top-five offense by almost any measurement, and they can beat you with both the pass and the run.Jared Goff is having a marvelous season, completing 67.8% of his passes at an average of 8.2 yards per attempt with 20 touchdown passes against six interceptions. He's third in the league behind only Brock Purdy and Joe Burrow in EPA per dropback, third behind only Purdy and Burrow in success rate and fourth behind only Purdy, Burrow and Patrick Mahomes in passer rating. His 8.2 yards-per-attempt average is the second-best of his tenure in Detroit, as are the 52.3% success rate and 107.7 passer rating.
He's of course blessed with one of the best skill-position corps in the league: Amon-Ra St. Brown is a picture of consistency; Jameson Williams is one of the most explosive threats in football; Sam LaPorta is a strong option and tight end; and Jahmyr Gibbs is the best running back in the NFL, leading the league in rushes, rushing yards, first downs, yards from scrimmage and total touchdowns.St. Brown often gets pigeonholed as a slot guy, but in reality he plays more outside (59.2% of snaps) than he does inside (39.8%), according to Tru Media, and he's equally capable of dominating defenses from either spot. He's Goff's first read more often than not because he runs a lot of short-area routes and the Lions like to get the ball out fairly quickly in their straight dropback game, where St. Brown is often the target. Williams is the guy the Lions turn toward when they're looking to test defenses in the intermediate and deep areas of the field. His 12.36-yard average route depth is fourth among 199 players who have run 100 or more routes this season, according to Tru Media, and he's generated an explosive gain (16-plus yards) on 26.3% of his targets, which ranks 17th among that same group of players. He and LaPorta are generally going to eat into each other's target shares in any given week, while St. Brown remains the more consistent top target.
The Bears' secondary is beatable, as Chicago ranks 22nd in net yards allowed per attempt, according to Pro-Football-Reference. Jaylon Johnson is not the same player he once was, Tyrique Stevenson is inconsistent, Kyler Gordon has barely played and Malik Muhammad has the ups and downs of a fourth-round rookie. If the Lions give Goff time to throw, he could feast on this group all afternoon.That's where Chicago's improved defensive line comes in. Since acquiring Jeffery Simmons, the Bears rank seventh in the league in EPA per dropback, per Tru Media, in large part because they have recorded a sack on 10.7% of opponent dropbacks. Prior to acquiring Simmons, Chicago's sack rate was 8.9%. That figure still ranked third in the league through seven weeks, but it's been much improved since the Bears dropped Simmons into the middle of the defensive line.Detroit is pretty strong up front, allowing pressure on only 32.3% of dropbacks, which ranks sixth in the NFL. The sack rate is a bit worse than that because Goff isn't the world's most mobile quarterback, but he's generally given adequate time to throw.
The Lions' run game is diverse, efficient and explosive. Gibbs is seventh in the NFL in yards per carry, fifth in the share of runs that gain five or more yards and second in explosive run rate, according to Tru Media. The Lions utilize him on plenty of inside runs, but he is obviously at his most dangerous when they get him on the perimeter and he can scoot past opposing defenders. is seventh in the NFL in yards per carry, fifth in the share of runs that gain five or more yards and second in explosive run rate, according to Tru Media. The Bears have allowed 4.7 yards per rush since acquiring Simmons, but that number is 5.9 per rush on attempts off tackle or off end, per Tru Media. Simmons plays inside, and the Bears can be tested on the perimeter.PredictionThese are two incredibly evenly matched teams, but it seems like Detroit has more matchup advantages offensively against Chicago's improved defense than the Bears do against the Lions' own improved unit. title: MLB rumors: Blue Jays narrow focus, Cardinals target pitching, plus more relievers off the board - CBS Sports
description: Here are your hot stove rumors for Thursday, Nov. 26
body:
Here are your hot stove rumors for Thursday, Nov. 26
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 26, 2026
                            
                    at
    9:44 am ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The pre-Thanksgiving, pre-lockout free agent frenzy arrived this week. Four of our top five, five of our top 10, and 20 of our top 50 free agents have already signed. You can be sure many more will come off the board between now and the expiration of the collective bargaining agreement at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. The pitching market in particular has really moved.Everyone is trying to squeeze in last minute signings and trades, and there could be a few deals on Thanksgiving. The hot stove pauses for no holiday. Here now are the Turkey Day rumors and moves.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Blue Jays will focus on offenseAfter landing Kaima Taira for five years and $80 million, the Blue Jays are expected to focus on adding offense, according to The Athletic. Toronto is not closing the door on adding more arms -- they remain engaged in the pitching market and have been connected to top free agent reliever Adrian Morejon -- but, with Taira aboard, offense is the greater priority moving forward.The Blue Jays ranked dead last in runs and home runs in 2026. Catcher (Alejandro Kirk), first base (Vladimir Guerrero Jr.), and third base (Kazuma Okamoto) are the only positions Toronto can reasonably bank on above-average offense, and that's only if Vlad Jr. rebounds from his awful season. The Blue Jays need at least a corner outfielder. A second baseman wouldn't hurt either.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Cardinals have interest in Bieber, Imanaga, MizeThe Cardinals have checked in on free agent starters Shota Imanaga and Casey Mize, reports the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. They've also touched base with Shane Bieber. All three are among our top 50 free agents. Imanaga in particular has been a popular free agent. He's been linked to several contenders and is plenty familiar with the NL Central given his time with the rival Cubs. Kyle Leahy, Quinn Mathews, Michael McGreevy, and Andre Pallante are penciled into rotation spots next year. Matthew Liberatore is still around, as is Richard Fitts for depth. St. Louis could use a veteran starter to help cover innings as they wait for top prospects Liam Doyle, Jurrangelo Cijntje, and Tekoah Roby to arrive. Someone to fill the role Dustin May filled in 2026, basically.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Nationals, Twins add relieversTwo 2027 postseason hopefuls added bullpen help late Wednesday evening. The Nationals agreed to a one-year, $5 million contract with lefty A.J. Puk, reports ESPN. There's an additional $2.5 million in incentives. Puk has not appeared in an MLB game since April 2025 due to UCL surgery and a shoulder capsule strain. Clearly, Washington expects him to be healthy in 2027.
The Twins, meanwhile, signed righty Kevin Ginkel, Puk's former teammate with the Diamondbacks, to a two-year deal worth $18 million, according to MLB.com. Ginkel, 33 in March, had a 5.01 ERA with Arizona over the last two years, though his under-the-hood indicators are much more promising. He'll join Yoendrys Gómez and Jeff Hoffman in Minnesota's late-inning mix.

title: Eight teams with the most to lose in Week 13: Oregon, Tennessee, UCLA face must-wins - CBS Sports
description: Rivalry Week always brings high stakes, but the pressure is even higher for these eight teams entering the final
body:
Rivalry Week always brings high stakes, but the pressure is even higher for these eight teams entering the final weekend of the regular season
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 26, 2026
                            
                    at
    10:06 am ET
                        
                •
            
            6 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Turkey Week provides plenty of rivalry games with College Football Playoff and conference championship implications, with things getting started Thursday night when Texas Tech hosts TCU.There are a couple of teams outside the CFP vying for bragging rights against a hated opponent and needing a reason to enter bowl season with some positivity. Another loss could stir up a hornet's nest at programs where the folks writing the checks are already asking hard questions.The bubble is crowded enough that even a team sitting inside the projected field can find itself on the wrong side of the cut line  -- looking at you, BYU. For most teams that don't have the luxury of playing themselves into the bracket during conference championship weekend, resumes are finalized in the next few days.Here's a look at eight teams with the most to lose during college football's final weekend of the regular season.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    8. South CarolinaIt'll be a long offseason for the Gamecocks if they go to Clemson and lose to Dabo Swinney's worst team in 15 years. Shane Beamer moved off the hot seat at midseason with four straight wins after the messaging following an 0-3 start in SEC play was that his buyout was too large to consider a move. That financial predicament hasn't changed, but the negative tenor surrounding the program has returned after his team swiftly fell out of the College Football Playoff discussion this month.Coming off consecutive 28-point losses to Arkansas and Georgia, the inconsistency that plagued Beamer's teams is back. He's now 6-14 over his last 20 contests against Power Four opponents, and a loss to Clemson would leave the Gamecocks at 6-6 overall with a third straight defeat. With pending NFL Draft decisions from Dylan Stewart and LaNorris Sellers, the outlook for 2027 is bleak. If the Gamecocks lose to the Tigers, Beamer will enter next year on the sport's hottest seat. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    7. Ohio StateFrom preseason No. 1 to four regular-season losses has been quite the stunning fall for the Buckeyes. Following Saturday's finale against Michigan, Ryan Day will face difficult coaching staff decisions to ensure a repeat failure doesn't happen in 2027. The defense has failed to replicate last season's production after losing a couple of first-rounders, and Arthur Smith's offensive playcalling has been a mixed bag.Ohio State moving on from Day, who led the program to a national championship just two years ago, is unlikely, but a loss to Michigan would amplify the noise. Considering Nebraska just snapped a 31-game skid against ranked teams at the Buckeyes' expense, blowing another tire in the season finale would devastate boosters. The last time Ohio State lost four games came in 2011, when the Buckeyes finished 6-7 in Luke Fickell's lone season before he was replaced by Urban Meyer. Ohio State would owe Day nearly $60 million if he's fired after playing The Team Up North, which even for the Buckeyes is quite cumbersome.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    6. BYUProjected as CBS Sports' first team out on Selection Sunday, the Cougars need style points against Cincinnati. The three-overtime win at Kansas did no favors for BYU's CFP case. 
The best path for the Big 12 to produce three teams in the bracket is for BYU to blow out the Bearcats and Texas Tech to take out the unbeaten Utes in the conference title game. BYU has a data point no other bubble squad holds -- a win over Notre Dame. Right now, that is essentially putting the Cougars on the same pedestal as the Red Raiders, despite Texas Tech's better record.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    5. Boise StateLast week's hard-to-fathom setback against San Diego State on the blue turf eliminated the Broncos' margin for error. There's a handful of other teams now in the picture after Boise State's rankings plunge Tuesday night. There's plenty of reason to believe Boise State will be the highest-ranked Group of Six team as long as it wins out and takes the Pac-12 Championship next weekend in a rematch with the Aztecs. 
Flex week against Colorado State certainly helps.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    4. IowaThe Hawkeyes have a chance at a sixth quality win with a victory Friday over Nebraska and, more importantly, could get to the Big Ten Championship with a little help in Week 13. Iowa's loss to Minnesota in late October is notable, but the Hawkeyes have won four straight since and are taking advantage of a favorable slate -- by Big Ten standards -- in the final weeks. Iowa was not included in our projected playoff bracket this week, but that changes with a win over the Huskers and a loss by Indiana or Oregon on Saturday. Ferentz wants no part of politicking to the selection committee, but he may need to say something after Friday's game to spark talks about why his team belongs if it gets to 10 wins.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    3. TennesseeThe Volunteers need not give the CFP selection committee any ammunition to further cloud its judgment about how it's power-ranking the SEC this season. Georgia is the obvious No. 1, but beyond the Bulldogs, Tennessee has an argument alongside Alabama -- a team the Vols beat by 16 points -- and Texas, which won inside Neyland Stadium by three. Tennessee has four wins over Power Four teams with above-.500 records, so a victory over Vanderbilt won't improve its resume. However, a loss in Nashville to an opponent at the bottom of the conference could put the Vols on the Selection Sunday cutline and leave them in the same boat as other three-loss teams, namely BYU.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    2. OregonOutside of Wake Forest, there's no hotter team in college football heading down the stretch than the Ducks. That's a credit to Dan Lanning holding this team together despite early-season struggles, the loss of quarterback Dante Moore and moving on from his offensive coordinator after seven games. 
Dylan Raiola was signed during the last portal cycle as Oregon's insurance policy for Moore, and he's been a godsend. He has 11 touchdown passes without an interception since his multi-turnover outing against UCLA on Oct. 10, and the Ducks are 5-1 since that loss with four consecutive wins.Saturday's home game against Washington is the most important of Lanning's tenure given the stakes: win, and the Ducks will play for a Big Ten Championship next weekend in Indianapolis. The Huskies are coming off an overtime upset of Indiana and are looking to spoil Oregon's potential CFP trip. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    1. UCLANo CFP contender needs a win more than the Bruins, given their tumble out of the top four Tuesday night. Down to third-team quarterback Madden Iamaleava after last week's loss to Michigan, UCLA must give the selection committee some belief that this team still belongs among the elites nearing the postseason. 
CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz reported Monday that the knee injury to Ty Dieffenbach does not appear to be season-ending, so that's promising. A win over USC at the Rose Bowl puts UCLA in the Big Ten Championship and gets the Bruins closer to the program's first CFP appearance, but a loss tanks the Big Ten's shot at being a three-bid league.The CFP precedent was set in 2023 when unbeaten Florida State was excluded from the final top four after its value was downgraded after losing starting quarterback Jordan Travis to a season-ending injury before the Seminoles' ACC Championship. This is not the same team with a second Iamaleava under center, who, before Saturday's appearance at Michigan, had appeared in only three other games this fall with minimal snaps. Dieffenbach's availability is paramount to UCLA's success moving forward.

        The Fantasy football playoffs are fast approaching, and with all 32 NFL teams in action in Week 12, lineup decisions aren't getting any easier. A loaded Thanksgiving slate, lingering injuries and evolving offensive roles present Fantasy managers with plenty to consider. While a full player pool offers more flexibility, it also forces managers to reconsider whether some of their usual starters still warrant a spot in their lineups.    That's where Dave Richard's Week 12 matchup breakdown comes in. From defensive coverages and pass-rush pressure to backfield workloads and target distribution, Dave examines the factors that could dictate Fantasy production. Whether you're weighing Emmett Johnson's upside, navigating Tyler Warren's declining production or deciding which quarterbacks to trust, we've got you covered with start/sit recommendations for every matchup. Jordan Love has posted north of 24 Fantasy points (six-point pass TDs) in just three games this year, and in all three he was pressured on less than 39.4% of his dropbacks. That's not going to quite be the case against Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald and the Rams, even if he has some of his starting O-linemen back. In the two games since Garrett's return, the Rams have totaled nine sacks and had a minimum sack rate of 10% -- and that's without blitzing much. That drives down the upside for Love, and it should also be mentioned that Tucker Kraft has a pitiful 13.5% target per route and 0.95 yards per route run rates when Love is pressured. The Rams have been fantastic at limiting tight end production all season and make Kraft a risky Fantasy choice.     Matthew Stafford has been among the league's fastest gunslingers this season and thus isn't affected by pass rush pressure unless it's quick. Not having two of his starting five offensive linemen -- both interior linemen -- should mean even more of an emphasis on quick throws. It's also worth noting that Stafford's average depth of throw has shrunk considerably since Week 5, and of the 13 passing touchdowns he's thrown since then, only one has come from outside of the red zone (and it was from 22 yards out against the Cardinals). The nine red-zone passing TDs the Packers have allowed ranks tied for ninth-best in the league this season, and their pass rush certainly has potential to get quick pressure on Stafford with Micah Parsons coming back. The quick-pass game Stafford will employ should benefit the target volume of his tight ends and running backs more than his receivers; the Packers' zone-heavy scheme should also encourage those throws. If the game is close, then Kyren Williams is the best running back to see extended touches, and Tyler Higbee is the Rams' runaway leader in tight end receiving stats and metrics, including route depth and average depth of target. You might start those guys with reasonable confidence, but the difficult circumstances for Stafford sink his chances of having a strong game.

And because the Lions really don't blitz all that often, it's reasonable to think Caleb Williams will be able to get some good numbers against what's been a shaky pass defense. Williams' play when pressured has been up and down all year, including last week. But also, as proven last week, when he's not pressured, he can make some flawless throws downfield. The Bears offensive line allowed a pass rush pressure rate of 33.3% or lower against the Seahawks and Saints this month, with the Saints blitzing 44% of their plays; the Bucs had to blitz 63% of the time just to get a 46% pass rush pressure rate on Williams (and it worked since he threw four INTs). Chicago has won four straight against the Lions, and Detroit's gone heavy on the blitz just once in those games. Williams should be in position to play well on Thanksgiving. Dallas has history with Joe Milton III, who, through two games, has not been a good passer overall and has just a 60% catchable-throw rate when pressured. I'd love to bank on Smith and Milton getting on the same page, but if this Dallas pass rush is going to affect Milton, then it could be another week of high volume and lower chances at huge stats for Smith.   Dallas Goedert is in an even worse spot: Overall, he's catching a target from Milton on 12.7% of his routes, but that percentage was an ugly 5.6% (one target!) last week. And when Milton's been pressured through two games, Goedert has seen one target total. One. In the two games since, they've basically ignored the run game as soon as they've fallen behind by at least a touchdown, the evidence of which is in Warren's touch numbers under that scoring circumstance -- no more than six carries in either game. Mike McCarthy said this week that the Steelers need to run the ball better and more often, and maybe it'll be easier for him to call more runs without having to appease a future Hall of Fame QB. But Fantasy managers shouldn't bank on that happening all game long, and even if it did, how much work might Warren lose out to Rico Dowdle? And it's not like Denver's offense has been weak, as they've scored at least 26 points in four straight games. That could mean more pass plays called once they fall behind. Warren's upside is obvious, but given the Steelers' issues at quarterback, on defense and along the offensive line, I'd hesitate to call him anything more than a risky No. 2 Fantasy option.  There's a downgrade in quarterback from current-day Aaron Rodgers to Mason Rudolph, but it's not by much. Rodgers averaged 9.3 yards downfield per throw with an 18.3% deep throw rate and a time-to-throw average of 2.85 seconds until Week 5, when he began going much shorter with his throws (5.8 yards downfield and an 11.1% deep throw rate) and got the ball out faster (2.6 seconds). These latter numbers are in line -- if not even smaller -- than what Rudolph has produced over the past two seasons in mop-up play. Rudolph also has career tendencies of leaning on his running backs (22% target rate) and tight ends (23%), both of which are perfect given the deficiencies in Denver's pass defense. But again, that's right where Rodgers was this season (21% to his RBs, 23% to his TEs). Maybe Rudolph can evade pass rush pressure better than Rodgers and lets a few more passes fly downfield, but it's tough to see him as any sort of upgrade for anyone in the Steelers offense.

Last week proved that the Texans are indeed capable of running the ball efficiently as David Montgomery averaged 4.1 yards per rush (4.9 in the first half). But that was in a one-sided blowout win over the Colts on a short week, and it was with Montgomery as the Texans' primary ball-carrier until the game was out of hand. The Ravens run defense is nothing to fear, but they should be capable of competing at a higher level than the Colts. More importantly, Woody Marks is expected back for the Texans and will cut into Montgomery's work. Montgomery played north of 60% of the snaps with Marks in just one of Houston's first four games, splitting third-down snaps almost evenly in three of four games and even splitting snaps near the goal line evenly (Montgomery was in on 3 of 3 in Week 1, Marks was in on 2 of 2 in Week 3). So even though the Ravens have let up the sixth-most PPR points to running backs over the past four weeks, the only substantial evidence that Montgomery will clearly be the better Texans Fantasy option is that he'll play a little more than Marks. We've seen just 10 games where Jonathan Taylor played with Anthony Richardson for at least 49% of the Colts snaps, all in 2024. In those 10 games, Taylor had 15-plus carries seven times, 10-plus PPR points seven times, 15-plus PPR points five times, and more than one reception one time. About one-third of Taylor's runs were read-option plays where Richardson chose in the moment to give Taylor the ball instead of keeping it himself, usually based on whether Richardson thought he had room to gain yards on his own. Richardson's barely played this year, but only two of the nine rushing plays called when he was on the field had elements of a read-option. It's kind of played out, plus even if the Colts used it, the Giants have done well (1.1 yards per rush allowed) against it.  After seeing at least 20 touches in seven of his first eight games, Taylor has had 18 or fewer in four straight including 15 or fewer in two blowout losses. There might not be much hesitation from the Colts to give D.J. Giddens about 30% of the snaps like they did Seth McGowan, but Taylor should be more of a fixture near the goal line -- whether he gets the ball or Richardson does remains a concern (along with if the Colts can actually get near the goal line). body:
Following Indiana's second loss and subsequent drop from No. 8 to No. 14 in the latest College Football Playoff rankings, cries of injustice are emanating from Bloomington. While Hoosiers coach Curt Cignetti has been busy retweeting Indiana's defenders, it's his own scheduling philosophy that is partially to blame for why IU is outside the at-large picture entering the regular season's final week. The defenders point out that Indiana has two wins against teams currently ranked inside the CFP's top 25 while No. 6 Alabama has zero such victories. They point out that the Hoosiers lost by a literal foot against a healthy Ohio State team and that their latest loss -- a 27-24 defeat at Washington -- came on the road in overtime.What they fail to mention is that Cignetti has gone out of his way to dodge quality nonconference opposition since arriving at IU after the 2023 season. Indiana is one of five Big Ten teams not playing a Power Four opponent (or Notre Dame) outside the conference this season. The year before Cignetti's arrival, Indiana played Louisville.Had the Hoosiers defeated Louisville in nonconference play this season instead of Western Kentucky, they would be five spots higher in our resume ranking this week and squarely in the CFP at-large picture entering the final week of the regular season.
Anyone comparing Indiana's resume to Alabama's also needs to consider who the losses came against. The Crimson Tide fell to No. 1 Georgia and to No. 5 Tennessee on the road. While Indiana's home loss to Ohio State falls in a similar category as those two, IU's loss at Washington does not.The Hoosiers receive a -0.59 hit to their resume score by losing to the Huskies, who are No. 37 in the CFB Metrics Consensus. It's a reflection of how the average No. 25-ranked team would beat Washington 59% of the time. You can't take losses like that and expect to make the playoff if you aren't counterbalancing them with big-time wins.That's what our resume score system does. It replicates the way the real committee evaluates resumes by assigning a value between -1 and 1 to each win/loss, based on the opponent's rank in the CFB Metrics Consensus and the likelihood that the average No. 25 team would win the game. When you compare Indiana's resume in this context to Alabama's resume -- or to the resume of any other team ahead of it in this week's CFP Rankings -- it gives you the answer as to why the Hoosiers are where they are.

        
            
                Most, least thankful teams this season: Oregon counts its blessings, while LSU feels holiday hangover
                
                    Austin Nivison                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Those values, which you see in parentheses below, are calculated based on where your opponents stand in the CFB Metrics Consensus, which is the "baseline" ranking. Without a baseline ranking, a resume ranking of this type would not be possible. So when you see Texas credited with a win over "No. 13" Ole Miss, it's not because the Rebels are 13th in the resume ranking, in the CFP Ranking or the AP poll. They aren't a top-15 team in any of those rankings. Though it's been a dreadful season for the Aggies, they still land in the top-40 of the CFB Metrics Consensus, which is the aggregation of 10 reputable power ratings. As was true last week, the Longhorns are still the only team with more than two Quad 1 wins…and they have four. But they aren't No. 1 from a power ratings perspective, which is why they aren't No. 1 in the CFP Rankings.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 2 GeorgiaRecord: 10-1Resume score: 3.38CFP Ranking: 1Quad 1 (2-0): W @ No. 4 Alabama (+0.91), W @ No. 13 Ole Miss (+0.73)Quad 2 (4-1): W vs. No. 20 Oklahoma (+0.52), L vs. No. 29 Auburn (-0.62), W vs. No. 24 Florida (N) (+0.51), W vs. No. 23 Missouri (+0.46), W @ No. 34 South Carolina (+0.44)Quad 3 (2-0): W @ No. 57 Arkansas (+0.26), W vs. No. 64 Vanderbilt (+0.15)Quad 4 (2-0): W vs. Tennessee State (0.00), W vs. No. 122 Western Kentucky (+0.02)What's left: vs. No. 82 Georgia Tech (Q4)Breakdown: Georgia's road win over Alabama is the third-most valuable victory obtained by anyone this season, per our rankings system. Not so fast; the 0.02 difference in their resume scores is not nearly enough to justify overriding a convincing head-to-head result. These rankings are raw scores calculated by a predetermined formula that doesn't factor in head-to-head results. The committee did the right thing by respecting head-to-head between two teams with nearly identical resume scores and similar power ratings.

By adding a win over USC, the Bruins should be able to solidify their place in the CFP. But without much depth on its resume, UCLA would have a tough case for inclusion at 10-2.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 12 OregonRecord: 8-3Resume score: 1.72CFP Ranking: 12Quad 1 (2-0): W @ No. 21 USC (+0.60), W @ No. 6 Ohio State (+0.87)Quad 2 (4-3): W vs. No. 35 Boise State (+0.33), L @ No. 26 Oklahoma State (-0.48), L vs. No. 17 UCLA (-0.42), W vs. No. 19 Nebraska (+0.54), L @ No. 40 Illinois (-0.62), W vs. No. 28 Northwestern (+0.39), W vs. No. 38 Michigan (+0.30)Quad 3 (1-0): W @ No. 70 Michigan State (+0.21)Quad 4 (1-0): W vs. Portland State (0.00)What's left: vs. No. 37 Washington (Q2)Breakdown: Oregon and Georgia are the only teams with a combined six Quad 1/Quad 2 victories. But with three Quad 2 losses dragging its resume down, Oregon likely needs to win the Big Ten title to reach the CFP. With a win over Washington this week, the Ducks will punch their ticket to Indianapolis and the conference championship game.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 13 IndianaRecord: 9-2Resume score: 1.61CFP Ranking: 14Quad 1 (1-1): W @ No. 19 Nebraska (+0.64), L vs. No. 6 Ohio State (-0.21)Quad 2 (3-1): W vs. No. 28 Northwestern (+0.39), W @ No. 38 Michigan (+0.40), W vs. No. 21 USC (+0.50), L @ No. 37 Washington (-0.59)Quad 3 (3-0): W vs. No. 67 North Texas (+0.14), W @ No. 92 Rutgers (+0.14), W vs. No. 59 Minnesota (+0.18)Quad 4 (2-0): W vs. Howard (0.00), W vs. No. 122 Western Kentucky (+0.02)What's left: vs. No. 77 Purdue (Q4)Breakdown: All Indiana had to do was beat Washington and Purdue, and it was likely headed to a third straight playoff appearance. But after faltering against the Huskies, the Hoosiers' resume is on thin ice. As you can see above, it's a costly defeat. IU would have benefited from playing a Power Four opponent in nonconference action, but Curt Cignetti's scheduling mantra has been to take the easy way out.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 14 IowaRecord: 9-2Resume score: 1.45CFP Ranking: 13Quad 1 (0-1): L vs. No. 6 Ohio State (-0.21)Quad 2 (5-0): W @ No. 38 Michigan (+0.40), W @ No. 37 Washington (+0.41), W vs. No. 27 Wisconsin (+0.40), W @ No. 28 Northwestern (+0.49), W @ No. 40 Illinois (+0.38)Quad 3 (1-1): W vs. No. 54 Iowa State (+0.20), L @ No. 59 Minnesota (-0.75)Quad 4 (3-0): W vs. No. 134 Northern Illinois (+0.01), W vs. UNI (0.00), W vs. No. 77 Purdue (+0.12)What's left: at No. 19 Nebraska (Q1)Breakdown: Iowa has cleaned up in Quad 2, notching true road wins over four teams inside the top-40 of the CFB Metrics Consensus. But a lack of high-end fare and an Oct. 24 loss at Minnesota is holding the Hawkeyes back. A road win at Nebraska to close the regular season would give the Hawkeyes a much-needed boost and give Iowa a better case for CFP inclusion.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 15 Ole MissRecord: 7-4Resume score: 1.44CFP Ranking: 22Quad 1 (2-3): W vs. No. 16 Louisville (N) (+0.64), W vs. No. 11 LSU (+0.69), L @ No. 3 Texas (-0.07), L vs. No. 1 Georgia (-0.08), L @ No. 20 Oklahoma (-0.38)Quad 2 (2-1): L @ No. 24 Florida (-0.44), W vs. No. 23 Missouri (+0.46), W vs. No. 29 Auburn (+0.38)Quad 3 (1-0): W @ No. 64 Vanderbilt (+0.23)Quad 4 (2-0): W vs. No. 133 Charlotte (+0.01), W vs. Wofford (0.00)What's left: vs. No. 53 Mississippi State (Q3)Breakdown: Once you get to this point, it's all 3/4 loss teams. This is another situation where defeating 6-5 LSU gives a big boost to an SEC team. The Tigers STILL power-rate at No. 11 in the CFB Metrics Consensus, the baseline ranking used to determine resume scores. It takes the aggregate of 10 different power ratings to paint the true picture of how difficult a team is to beat. Between that win and a neutral-site victory over a Louisville team that has turned out to be pretty good, Ole Miss would be in great shape to make a 24-team playoff this time next year.

body:
Happy Thanksgiving, baseball enthusiasts! As the holiday name   suggests, Thursday is a day to be grateful for the good things that     have  happened and the good things to come. Non-football sports are   often secondary on Turkey Day, but  baseball is a way  of life as much    as it  is an interest. It's a  companion, there with you every  night  during the  summer.        On this Thanksgiving holiday, here  is one thing fans    of   each MLB team can be thankful for this year. Mike Axisa handled the American League and Dayn Perry tackled the National League. Now sit back, loosen up your      belt, and take a gander as you digest.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Arizona Diamondbacks  The Diamondbacks have been tantalizingly close to the playoffs the last two years. Know what might get them over the hump in 2027? The return of Corbin Burnes. Their on-paper ace returned from Tommy John surgery in time to make three subpar starts this past season, but his true comeback – one that brings with it the hope of a return to peak form – will come next season. Assuming all goes well, Burnes will be a huge boon to the Snakes' hopes in 2027.    
                            
    
                                                
                    
      (Sacramento) Athletics  On the field, 2026 went about as poorly as possible for the Athletics. Almost every core player missed significant time with injury and their pitching was wretched. At a time when the A's are supposed to be building up for their move to Las Vegas, they went from 76 wins in 2025 to 64 wins in 2026. Yeesh. The good news is the A's have new leadership. President of baseball operations Taylor Smith comes over from the Red Sox and general manager Cam Castro joins from the Brewers, which are two pretty good teams to emulate. The Athletics needed new voices and a fresh perspective in the front office, and they have it now.  

                            
    
                                                
                    
      Atlanta Braves  For the Braves, their gratitude comes from reflection. Last season, they rebounded from the disappointments of 2025 to log 94 wins and claim the National League East title. As well, they won a postseason series for the first time since 2021. On top of that, the Braves exacted revenge upon their NL East rivals, the Phillies, by defeating them in the Wild Card Series. That comes after the Phillies eliminated the Braves in 2022 and 2023.    
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Baltimore Orioles  The Orioles again failed to reach the postseason this past season and they traded away Adley Rutschman, once the face of the franchise, at the deadline. It was a disappointing year through and through. Year 1 of the Pete Alonso experience certainly went well, though. He led all first basemen with 5.0 WAR, led the league with 43 home runs and 113 RBI, and finished fifth in the AL MVP voting. Right-handed power is in shockingly short supply these days and the O's have one of the very best right-handed power hitters in their game anchoring their lineup. Big money free agent signings should all work out as well as Alonso did in 2026.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Boston Red Sox  There is a lot to like about the Red Sox at the major-league level. They've added Jake Bauers, Curtis Mead, and Adley Rutschman to their lineup in the last four months or so, and the rotation is stacked with Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suárez, and Payton Tolle. Boston also has one of the very best prospects in the game knocking on the door in Franklin Arias. The shortstop of the future (and, very soon, the present) slashed .323/.400/.557 with 25 home runs and only 74 strikeouts in 117 games between Double-A and Triple-A in 2027. Not-so-bold prediction: Arias will be the Red Sox's Opening Day shortstop next year. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
      Chicago Cubs  The Cubs are very much in contending mode right now, even if their last two trips to the postseason haven't yielded anything close to the desired results. The foundation, though, is there, and it's Pete Crow-Armstrong. Not only is he one of the best all-around and most electric performers in the games, but he's also just 24 years of age. Best of all, at least from the Cubs' standpoint, he's under contract through 2032 at what will almost certainly turn out to be deep-bargain rates.    
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Chicago White Sox  Here is the complete list of right-handed hitters to hit 30 home runs, walk 100 times, and strike out fewer than 130 times since the 2020 pandemic season: Miguel Vargas in 2026. That's it. The last righty hitters to do it before Vargas were Alex Bregman and Mike Trout in 2019. Munetaka Murakami may have gotten the headlines, but Vargas was the White Sox's best player this year. He's a legitimate star with a special blend of contact, power, and plate discipline. Getting Vargas for spare parts (Erick Fedde, Michael Kopech, Tommy Pham) at the 2025 trade deadline has proven to be a terrific move by POBO Chris Getz.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Cincinnati Reds  The Reds are a bit rudderless right now, but their rooters can be grateful that sparkling shortstop Elly De La Cruz is on the roster. With a 30-30 season and a breakout campaign with the bat freshly behind him, De La Cruz is poised to become an MVP candidate as a 25-year-old in 2027. Whether that's with Cincy long-term or as a blockbuster trade piece that nets the Reds a true haul remains to be determined.    

                            
    
                                                
                    
      Cleveland Guardians  It has never been a question of talent with Chase DeLauter. He had just been held back by injuries, most notably a series of foot injuries, dating back to his time at James Madison. This year, though, DeLauter stayed on the field and turned in an excellent rookie season: .287/.363/.457 with 16 home runs and only 82 strikeouts in 133 games. The underlying data (exit velocity, etc.) is impressive. Once DeLauter learns how to pull a few more balls in the air rather than push them the other way, he'll be a monster. The Guardians are in perpetual need of offense and DeLauter looks like a long-term keeper in the middle of the lineup.   
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Colorado Rockies  Rare is the primary catcher who tops 40 home runs in a season, but that's exactly what Hunter Goodman did in 2026. That makes him a hugely valuable presence moving forward. Whether that's as a Rockie as the modernized front office gets them up to speed or as a blockbuster trade target for other teams is TBD. Either way, he's a needle-mover. For those curious, 25 of his 41 home runs last season came away from Coors Field.    
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Detroit Tigers  It ultimately did not happen, but as late as August, Kevin McGonigle had a chance to finish with the third-highest WAR by a rookie position player in the Expansion Era (since 1961), behind only Mike Trout and Aaron Judge. Even without that admittedly obscure distinction, McGonigle was sensational in 2026, slashing .278/.376/.430 with 18 home runs and nearly as many walks (95) as strikeouts (100). He won American League Rookie of the Year and finished seventh in the AL MVP voting. Best of all, the Tigers wisely locked McGonigle up to an eight-year, $150 million extension in April. That will keep him in Detroit through 2034 and it already looks like a bargain.  

                            
    
                                                
                    
      Houston Astros  I don't think there's a better or more imposing hitter in baseball than Yordan Alvarez. He's so big and scary! Years of near-MLB-best performance finally culminated in an AL MVP award this season as Air Yordan slashed .316/.432/.601 with 42 home runs and nearly as many walks (109) as strikeouts (120). Here's something that flew under the radar: Alvarez was intentionally walked 33 times, second most in American League history behind Aaron Judge's 36 in 2025. You know you're good when teams put you on intentionally that much. The Astros eked out an AL West title this past season and Alvarez was the single biggest reason.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Kansas City Royals  Bobby Witt Jr. turned in another terrific season and finished second among all players with 7.0 WAR. He's a given here. Now he has a great running mate in Jac Caglianone, who reined in the swing-and-miss and slashed .289/.340/.494 with 23 home runs. His exit velocity and hard-hit data are among the very best in baseball. All Caglianone needs to do to become one of the game's truly elite hitters is reduce his ground ball rate, which was an elevated 46.3% in 2026. You'd like to see that number down around 38% (if not lower) for a guy with this much power. Point is, the Royals have a second building block in their lineup.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Los Angeles Angels  The Arte Moreno Reign of Error is over. Moreno has agreed to sell the Angels to Stan Kroenke for the tidy sum of $4 billion, and, if nothing else, it really can't get any worse. I mean, the Halos lost 100 games for the first time in franchise history in 2026. Kroenke's other franchises have all won a title recently (Arsenal F.C. in the English Premier League, the NBA's Denver Nuggets, the NHL's Colorado Avalanche, etc.) and tend to be smart, well-run organizations. It will take some time to turn the Angels around, but at least now there's some hope. Under Moreno, there wasn't.  

                            
    
                                                
                    
      Los Angeles Dodgers  The Dodgers have plenty of veteran star power on the roster, fronted of course by Shohei Ohtani. Now, though, they have some young upside on the way in outfielder Josue De Paula, who's one of the top prospects in all of baseball. The 21-year-old lefty batsman has star upside at the plate, and coming off a highly successful cuppa coffee in 2026, he's poised for a bigger role and maybe Rookie of the Year honors in 2027.    
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Miami Marlins  As the Marlins methodically work their way back toward relevance, Otto Lopez has emerged as A Dude. Over the last three seasons, the shortstop has increased his WAR from 2.8 in 2024 to 3.6 in 2025 to last season's mark of 6.1. Going into his age-28 season, Lopez is operating at peak and may be the most underrated player in baseball right now.    
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Milwaukee Brewers  This one's not challenging. The Brewers are fresh off the first World Series title in franchise history, and those credentials are burnished by a 2026 regular season that saw them post the best record and best run differential in all of baseball. It's not "just" a championship; it's dominance en route to that championship. Fans of the Crew should thus be the most grateful of all right about now.    

                            
    
                                                
                    
      Minnesota Twins  This month was pleasantly surprising and productive for the Twins. First, Ryan Jeffers accepted the $23.15 million qualifying offer, and I'm not sure anyone expected that. Getting him back on a one-year contract is a win even if it is a big salary. And second, Sonny Gray returned to Minnesota on a two-year deal worth $55 million (with an opt out). Just like that, the Twins welcomed back a key middle-of-the-order hitter and stalwart catcher, and upgraded their rotation significantly. This past season was a major disappointment, for sure, but I don't think you need to try all that hard to see this team contending for the AL Central title in 2027.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
      New York Mets  Mets fans, your team just signed far and away the top free agent on the market in ace and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. Yes, the cost was high, but the Mets now have at the front of the rotation perhaps the best pitcher in all of baseball. The pressure is on both team and player, but the pairing is made to order for a team that needed such a presence on the staff.    
                            
    
                                                
                    
      New York Yankees  I'm partial to Ron Guidry's 1978, but the case can be made that Cam Schlittler just turned in the greatest pitching season in Yankees history once you adjust for era. His 215 ERA+ is in fact a franchise record for a qualified pitcher, besting Guidry's 208 ERA+ during that 1978 season. Regardless of where Schlittler's Cy Young campaign ranks historically, he emerged as a bona fide ace in his first full MLB season, one in which he proved himself to be a Red Sox killer (always a plus for a Yankee). The Yankees turned a seventh-round draft pick into a front-of-the-rotation starter. If you can't be thankful about that, what can you?  

                            
    
                                                
                    
      Philadelphia Phillies  The Phillies are finally willing to move the defensively deficient Trea Turner off of shortstop. That's a welcome development. Speaking of welcome developments, veteran shortstop Corey Seager of the Texas Rangers is reportedly willing to waive his no-trade clause to join the Phils. That would be a great targeted strike by Dave Dombrowski and help keep Philly's contending window open a bit longer. And even if not, at least they're trying.
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Pittsburgh Pirates  Shortstop Konnor Griffin held his own as a 20-year-old rookie last season, putting up a 2.1 WAR in just 80 games. It's rare enough to even reach the majors at such an age, let alone provide value. Griffin looks like a regular All-Star selection and occasional MVP candidate for years and years to come, and the Pirates have secured his services through the 2034 season.    
                            
    
                                                
                    
      St. Louis Cardinals  It's about the future in St. Louis. Under lead operator Chaim Bloom and the built-out player-development program, the Cardinals in short order have gone from a mediocre farm system to one of the very best in the game. Pair those incoming talents with in-place youngsters like JJ Wetherholt and Jordan Walker, and the future for the Cardinals is shimmering.    

                            
    
                                                
                    
      San Diego Padres  There's no replacing the late Peter Seidler, the beloved Padres owner who distinguished himself by caring about and committing to winning more than almost any other owner in the game. Now, though, new owners José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones have signaled they, too, have bold intentions with the Padres. They were seriously in the bidding for Tarik Skubal, and while they didn't land the top free agent, their presence in the fray suggests payroll retrenchment isn't on the way in San Diego. That's encouraging.    
                            
    
                                                
                    
      San Francisco Giants  The Giants seem forever in need of offense lately, and rookie Bryce Eldridge in 2026 gave them value in the present and promise for the future. One of the top offensive prospects in baseball coming into 2026, he proved himself and then some after arriving in San Fran to put up a 133 OPS+ in 107 games. That was good for seventh place in the National League Rookie of the Year vote. He's looking like a middle-of-the-order presence for years to come, and that's just what this flagging organization needs.    
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Seattle Mariners  Gosh, what a disappointing season for the Mariners. They went from Game 7 of the ALCS in 2025 -- five outs away from their first pennant! -- to 76 wins and failing to reach the postseason in the sad sack American League in 2026. Woof. On the bright side, Kade Anderson, the No. 3 pick in the 2025 Draft, quickly emerged as baseball's top pitching prospect and made seven solid big league starts late in the season. His minor-league performance was simply incredible: 1.06 ERA with 135 strikeouts and only 13 walks in 93 ⅓ Double-A innings. Anderson's emergence allowed the Mariners to trade Bryce Miller for Maikel Garcia, a trade I loved for Seattle.  

                            
    
                                                
                    
      Tampa Bay Rays  Tobias Myers for Junior Caminero in November 2021 is already one of the most lopsided, landscape-altering trades of the generation, and Caminero has only played two full seasons. He hit 40-plus home runs in those two seasons, joining Hall of Famer Eddie Mathews as the only players in history to hit 40 homers twice before their age-23 season. Caminero is one of the very best hitters in the game and the Rays stole him away from the Guardians for a depth arm in Myers, who never threw a single pitch for Cleveland. A heist of seismic proportions.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Texas Rangers  If not for February UCL surgery, top prospect Sebastian Walcott likely would have made his MLB debut this summer. He returned to the field in mid-July and didn't miss a beat: .325/.401/.590 with 10 home runs in 41 minor-league games while reaching Triple-A. Walcott mashed in another 16 games in the Arizona Fall League as well. The UCL surgery was a tough break, but Walcott had a smooth recovery and will soon join a Rangers team that needs all the offensive help it can get after finishing 25th in runs in 2026.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Toronto Blue Jays  I could go with something cheeky like "2026 is over (especially for Vladimir Guerrero Jr.)," but nah, we'll instead give Dylan Cease and Kazuma Okamoto their flowers for tremendous first seasons with the Blue Jays. Cease had the league's highest strikeout rate and finished second in the Cy Young voting in Year 1 of his seven-year, $210 million contract. Okamoto slugged 33 home runs and looked better at third base than I think even the Blue Jays expected. He signed a four-year, $60 million deal last offseason. A lot went wrong for Toronto this past season, but Cease and Okamoto went very, very right.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Washington Nationals  James Wood. There are many reasons for Nats partisans to be encouraged about the current direction of the organization and the young talent in place, and then there's Wood. Wood just recently turned 24, and he has a career OPS+ of 134 in more than 1,600 plate appearances at the highest level. If there's a candidate for "the National League's answer to Yordan Alvarez" right now, then it's Wood.

schema.headline: What all 30 MLB teams have to be thankful for this year - CBS Sports
